name: PriorityClass & preemption
objective: CKA › Workloads & Scheduling. A PriorityClass stamps pods with a priority value; the scheduler places higher-priority pods first and, on a full node, will PREEMPT (evict) lower-priority pods to make room. Create PriorityClasses and use them, then watch a high-priority pod preempt low-priority ballast on a full node.

questions.title: Create PriorityClasses and use one
questions.teach:
A **PriorityClass** is a cluster-scoped object mapping a name to an integer `value` (higher = more important). A pod opts in with `priorityClassName`; the admission controller copies the number into the pod's `.spec.priority`. The scheduler orders the pending queue by priority and uses it to decide preemption.

**Gotcha:** `globalDefault: true` applies a PriorityClass to pods that don't name one (only one default allowed). Values above 1,000,000,000 are reserved for system-critical classes.
questions.prompt:
Create two PriorityClasses: `high-priority` (value `1000000`) and `low-priority` (value `100`). Then in namespace `priority-learn` run pod `important` (image `nginx:1.25`) with `priorityClassName: high-priority`.

Target: PriorityClass `high-priority` has value 1000000; pod `important` uses it and its `.spec.priority` is `1000000`.
questions.hint: `kubectl create priorityclass high-priority --value=1000000` and `--value=100` for low-priority. Then a pod with `spec.priorityClassName: high-priority`. Check: `kubectl -n priority-learn get pod important -o jsonpath='{.spec.priority}'`.
questions.solution:
kubectl create priorityclass high-priority --value=1000000 2>/dev/null
kubectl create priorityclass low-priority --value=100 2>/dev/null
kubectl create namespace priority-learn 2>/dev/null
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: important, namespace: priority-learn }
spec:
  priorityClassName: high-priority
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
YAML

verification.description: PriorityClass high-priority=1000000 and pod important uses it (.spec.priority=1000000)

questions.eli5:
Imagine a busy hospital waiting room. Everyone who walks in gets a **triage number** written on their wristband — a plain integer. The bigger the number, the sooner you get seen. A **PriorityClass** is the hospital's official chart that says *"a 'heart-attack' wristband is worth 1,000,000 points; a 'stubbed-toe' wristband is worth 100 points."* You define that chart once, cluster-wide, and give each entry a name.

When a pod checks in, it doesn't write its own number — it just says *"give me the `high-priority` wristband"* (`priorityClassName: high-priority`). A little gatekeeper at the door (the admission controller) looks up the chart and **stamps the real number onto the pod** (`.spec.priority = 1000000`). Now the scheduler, which runs the waiting room, always calls the highest number first.

That's it: you make named tiers once, and pods point at a tier by name instead of memorizing numbers.

**Watch out for:**

- **The chart is cluster-wide, not per-namespace.** `kubectl create priorityclass` has no `-n` flag — one set of tiers for the whole cluster.
- **Check the stamped number, not the name.** Grading looks at `.spec.priority` (the integer), which the gatekeeper copied in. `kubectl -n priority-learn get pod important -o jsonpath='{.spec.priority}'`.
- **`globalDefault: true`** gives a wristband to anyone who forgot to ask for one — and **only one** PriorityClass in the whole cluster can be the default.
- **Numbers above 1,000,000,000 are reserved** for Kubernetes' own system-critical pods. Don't use them for your apps.
- Higher value = more important. Pick the value deliberately; it's just an integer and the scheduler compares them directly.
questions.deepDive:
## PriorityClass — full rundown

### Mental model
A **PriorityClass** is a **cluster-scoped** object that maps a *name* to an integer *value*. Pods reference it by name via `priorityClassName`; at admission time the `Priority` admission controller resolves the name and **copies the integer into the pod's immutable `.spec.priority`**. The scheduler then uses that number to (a) order the pending queue (high first) and (b) decide preemption.

> Priority is just a number the scheduler compares. The PriorityClass is the human-friendly label that produces that number.

### Create a PriorityClass
```bash
# imperative (fastest in the exam)
kubectl create priorityclass high-priority --value=1000000
kubectl create priorityclass low-priority  --value=100
```

```yaml
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata:
  name: high-priority          # cluster-scoped — NO namespace
value: 1000000                  # required integer; higher = more important
globalDefault: false           # at most ONE class may set this true
description: "For latency-critical web pods"
preemptionPolicy: PreemptLowerPriority   # default; or Never
```

### Use it on a pod
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: important, namespace: priority-learn }
spec:
  priorityClassName: high-priority   # name reference
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
# after admission: .spec.priority == 1000000 (set for you)
```

### Fields
| Field | Scope | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `value` | required | Integer priority. Higher wins. Can be negative. |
| `globalDefault` | optional | If `true`, applied to pods with **no** `priorityClassName`. Only **one** allowed cluster-wide. |
| `preemptionPolicy` | optional | `PreemptLowerPriority` (default) or `Never` (schedule by priority but never evict others). |
| `description` | optional | Free text. |
| `.spec.priorityClassName` (pod) | optional | Name of the class the pod opts into. |
| `.spec.priority` (pod) | read-only | Integer copied in by admission; **immutable**. |

### Built-in / reserved classes
| Name | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `system-cluster-critical` | 2000000000 | Cluster-critical add-ons |
| `system-node-critical` | 2000001000 | Highest; node-critical (e.g. kube-proxy) |

Values **≥ 1000000000 (one billion)** are reserved for system-critical workloads — don't assign them to app PriorityClasses.

### Inspect
```bash
kubectl get priorityclass                    # list all, shows VALUE / GLOBAL-DEFAULT
kubectl describe priorityclass high-priority
kubectl -n priority-learn get pod important \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.priority}{"\n"}'        # the stamped integer
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Cluster-scoped.** `kubectl create priorityclass -n foo` is wrong — there is no namespace. Pods are namespaced; the class is not.
- **Grade on `.spec.priority`, not the name.** The number is what matters to the scheduler and to validators.
- **Default is a singleton.** Setting `globalDefault: true` on a second class is rejected while another default exists.
- **`.spec.priority` is immutable.** You can't edit a running pod's priority; delete and recreate.
- **Deleting a PriorityClass** does not retroactively change pods that already used it (their `.spec.priority` stays), but new pods referencing the gone name fail admission.
- **Reserved range:** keep app values well below one billion.
- Priority affects **scheduling order and preemption only** — it is **not** a QoS/eviction-under-memory-pressure class (that's `requests`/`limits`).

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl create priorityclass high-priority --value=1000000
kubectl create priorityclass low-priority  --value=100
# pod: spec.priorityClassName: high-priority
kubectl -n priority-learn get pod important -o jsonpath='{.spec.priority}'   # -> 1000000
```

questions.title: Preemption: evict low-priority to fit high
questions.teach:
When a higher-priority pod can't schedule because a node is full, the scheduler **preempts** — it evicts one or more lower-priority pods on a node to make room, then places the high-priority pod. Preempted pods are deleted (and recreated by their controller, where they may sit Pending).

**Gotcha:** preemption only fires when there's genuinely no room — the scheduler picks the fewest/lowest-priority victims. A pod can opt out of causing preemption with `preemptionPolicy: Never` (it still schedules by priority, just never evicts others).
questions.prompt:
Setup pinned two low-priority `ballast` pods (PriorityClass `demo-low`) onto `$W1`, filling it. Create a high-priority pod `vip` in `priority-learn` (image `nginx:1.25`, `priorityClassName: demo-high`, `nodeSelector prio-demo=yes`, CPU request `1000m`) — the scheduler must preempt a ballast pod to place it.

Target: `vip` is `Running` on `$W1`, and the scheduler preempted at least one `ballast` pod (fewer remain running).
questions.hint: Create `vip` with `priorityClassName: demo-high`, `nodeSelector: {prio-demo: yes}`, and `resources.requests.cpu: 1000m`. The node is full of demo-low ballast, so the scheduler evicts one to fit vip. Watch: `kubectl -n priority-learn get pods -w`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: vip, namespace: priority-learn, labels: { role: vip } }
spec:
  priorityClassName: demo-high
  nodeSelector: { prio-demo: "yes" }
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    resources: { requests: { cpu: 1000m } }
YAML
kubectl -n priority-learn get pods -o wide -w

verification.description: vip Running on $W1 after preempting a low-priority ballast pod

questions.eli5:
Picture a small parking garage (a node) that's completely full of cheap economy cars (the `ballast` pods — low priority). A VIP in a limo (`vip` — high priority) pulls up and *must* park in **this specific garage** (because of its `nodeSelector`), but there's no free space.

The attendant (the scheduler) looks around and says: *"I have a VIP who outranks these economy cars, and the garage is full. I'll tow out the cheapest car to make room."* That towing is **preemption** — the scheduler **evicts** a lower-priority pod so the higher-priority one fits. It politely picks the **fewest, lowest-ranked victims** needed, not everyone.

The towed economy car isn't destroyed forever — if something owns it (a Deployment/ReplicaSet), a new copy gets created and goes back to the waiting line, possibly stuck `Pending` because the garage is still full.

**Watch out for:**

- **Preemption only fires when there's genuinely no room.** If the car fits, nobody gets towed. Here the CPU request (`1000m`) plus the pinning (`nodeSelector prio-demo=yes`) is what makes the node truly full for `vip`.
- **The victim is chosen by lowest priority**, and only as many as needed are evicted.
- **It's about scheduling, not running pods under memory pressure** — preemption happens at *schedule time* to make space.
- A pod with **`preemptionPolicy: Never`** still jumps the queue by priority but will **never tow anyone** — it just waits for space.
- The evicted ballast may linger `Pending` afterward — that's expected; the node is full.
- Grading checks that `vip` is **Running on `$W1`** *and* that **fewer ballast pods remain** — i.e. a real eviction happened, not just a reshuffle.
questions.deepDive:
## Preemption — full rundown

### Mental model
When a pod **cannot be scheduled** anywhere that satisfies its constraints because candidate nodes are **full**, the scheduler checks whether evicting **lower-priority** pods on one node would let the pending pod fit. If so, it **preempts**: deletes the victim pod(s) (respecting graceful termination) and schedules the high-priority pod there.

> Priority orders the *queue*. Preemption is what priority *does* to running pods when there's no free room.

### The flow in this scenario
1. `$W1` is labeled `prio-demo=yes` and packed with two `ballast` pods (PriorityClass `demo-low`) that reserve its CPU.
2. `vip` requests `cpu: 1000m`, `priorityClassName: demo-high`, and `nodeSelector: {prio-demo: "yes"}` — it can *only* go to `$W1`.
3. `$W1` has no free CPU → `vip` is unschedulable by normal filtering.
4. Scheduler runs **preemption**: finds `demo-low` pods (priority lower than `demo-high`) whose removal frees enough CPU, picks the **fewest / lowest** needed, evicts them.
5. `vip` schedules onto `$W1`. The evicted ballast is recreated by its owner and may sit `Pending`.

### Manifest
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: vip
  namespace: priority-learn
  labels: { role: vip }
spec:
  priorityClassName: demo-high
  nodeSelector: { prio-demo: "yes" }     # forces the full node
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.25
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 1000m }           # makes the node genuinely full
```

### How the victim is chosen
The scheduler aims to disturb the cluster as little as possible:
- Only pods with **lower priority** than the incoming pod are candidates.
- It evicts the **minimum set** that frees enough room, preferring the **lowest-priority** pods.
- It respects **PodDisruptionBudgets** on a best-effort basis (will violate them if necessary to schedule a higher-priority pod).
- Victims get their normal **graceful termination** period.

### preemptionPolicy
| Policy | Queue ordering by priority | Can it evict others? |
|---|---|---|
| `PreemptLowerPriority` (default) | ✅ | ✅ |
| `Never` | ✅ | ❌ (waits for space instead) |

Set on the PriorityClass:
```yaml
preemptionPolicy: Never
```

### Observe it
```bash
kubectl -n priority-learn get pods -o wide -w        # watch ballast vanish, vip appear
kubectl -n priority-learn get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | grep -i preempt
kubectl -n priority-learn describe pod vip | sed -n '/Events/,$p'
#  Normal  Preempted  ...  Preempted by pod vip ... on node $W1
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **No pressure, no preemption.** If the pod fits without evicting anyone, nothing is preempted. The CPU request + nodeSelector are what create the squeeze.
- **Requests, not limits, drive scheduling.** The scheduler sums `requests`; set them deliberately to fill the node.
- **Victims are recreated and may stay `Pending`.** That's expected — the node is still full for the lower tier.
- **`preemptionPolicy: Never`** = priority ordering without collateral eviction. Easy to confuse with "no priority."
- Preemption is **schedule-time**; it is distinct from **kubelet eviction** under node memory/disk pressure (that uses QoS classes from requests/limits).
- **Cross-node**: the scheduler preempts on **one** node to fit the pod there; it won't scatter the pending pod across nodes.
- **PDBs are best-effort** during preemption — a high-enough priority pod can still cause a violation.

### Quick reference
```bash
# vip: high priority + request + nodeSelector onto a full node
kubectl -n priority-learn get pods -o wide -w
kubectl -n priority-learn get events | grep -i preempt
kubectl -n priority-learn get pod vip -o jsonpath='{.spec.nodeName}'   # == $W1
```
